script: About $71,000 gets you the shape of a Le Mans class winner without the V12. This Ferrari 250 GTO Tribute started as a 1972 Datsun 240Z before someone fitted Blue Ray GT Engineering's Rhino GT body kit. The original won its class and finished second overall at Le Mans in 1962, the same year Ferrari introduced it. Ferrari only built 36. Instead of the Datsun's straight six you get a 350 cubic inch Chevrolet small block with Holley's self-tuning Sniper 2 fuel injection. You work the Tremec through an exposed metal gate and all six gears drive the rear wheels. The real GTO had five. Those 16-inch wire wheels come off with one central spinner per wheel instead of a ring of lug nuts. Would you spend that money on a Le Mans lookalike with Chevy power, or are you in the camp that says leave the Datsun alone?

sections.Highlights: THIS... is a Ferrari 250 GTO Tribute, finished in Rosso Corsa with a Cuoio interior. This is a replica of the Ferrari 250 GTO that's based on a Datsun 240Z, built using a Blue Ray GT Engineering Rhino GT kit, and registered as a 1972 Datsun in Quebec, Canada. It's reportedly powered by a Chevrolet-sourced 350-cubic-inch V8 engine linked to a Tremec T56 6-speed gated manual transmission. A partial list of notable currently installed equipment reported by the seller includes a Holley Sniper 2 electronic fuel injection system, 16-inch knock-off wire wheels, leather upholstery, and a gated shifter. The Ferrari 250 GTO was produced from 1962 to 1964 as a homologation special for GT-class racing, with just 36 examples built. Powered by a 3.0-liter V12 and developed for competition use, it achieved success in events like the Tour de France, Targa Florio, and 24 Hours of Le Mans. Its combination of performance, rarity, and design has made it one of the most valuable collector cars in the world, which explains why replicas have become relatively common. Power comes from a 350-cubic-inch V8. Output is sent to the rear wheels via a 6-speed gated manual transmission.
